title: Paper Discussion Prompts
text:
How this works. In groups of 3–4, discuss each paper for about 4 minutes using the prompts below. Every group gets the same prompts. Then a few groups report back. Jot down one idea per prompt; you don’t need to cover them all.
For every paper, start with the syllabus’s reading questions: What is the question? How do the authors investigate it? What is the most important evidence?

title: Paper Discussion Prompts
text:
Measure · Fransen et al. (2023)
Taking stock of the implementation gap in climate policy. Nature Climate Change.
The idea. The “implementation gap” has two parts: a policy adoption gap (pledges vs. projected emissions under adopted policies, from Climate Action Tracker) and a policy outcome gap (what adopted policies should achieve vs. what they do achieve). The outcome gap can’t be measured directly, so the authors compare policy-strength scores (CCPI, 2018–2022) with a 2023 outcome index.
Warm-up. Pick one concept: climate ambition, state capacity to implement climate policy, inclusivity of a COP, or vulnerability to climate change. Write down (1) an indicator, (2) a data source, and (3) one thing your indicator misses.

How did the authors get a number for something that can only be measured after the fact?
Validity: does a CCPI policy score capture implementation?
Reliability: CCPI is partly built from expert assessments. Would different experts score the same country the same way?
Where does the outcome gap show up in the data? (Hint: in how countries scatter around the expected diagonal.)

title: Paper Discussion Prompts
text:
Map · Xie et al. (2025)
Tracing inclusivity at UNFCCC conferences through side events and interest group dynamics. Nature Climate Change.
The idea. UNFCCC records of COP side events, COP9–COP28 (2003–2023): titles, descriptions and host organizations. Topic modelling traces themes; network analysis maps who co-hosts energy events (COP17–28).

What is one observation? An event? An organization? A link between two organizations?
Population or sample? Every registered side event is included. What isn’t? (Unregistered events, country pavilions, the negotiating rooms themselves…)
Measurement: how does “inclusivity” become a number? What would you use?
Variation: what differs across COPs and across actor groups? Is that enough to compare them fairly?
Limits: does a central position in a network mean influence over negotiated outcomes?

title: Paper Discussion Prompts
text:
Model · Tennant, Davies & Tennant (2024)
Determinants of access to climate finance: Nuanced insights for SIDS and other vulnerable economies. World Development.
The idea. Two stages: do donors use different criteria to decide who is eligible for climate finance than to decide how much each eligible country gets? And do small island developing states (SIDS) get more or less than their vulnerability and adaptive capacity would justify?

Measure: where do the finance numbers come from, and who reports them? (Donors report to the OECD and tag their own projects.)
Is “more than justified by vulnerability” a causal claim or a comparison? What does “justified” assume?
Confounders: what factors does the model hold constant? What could still be missing?
Inference: the data cover nearly every recipient. What do the p-values mean here?
Design: if you wanted a causal answer, what comparison would you look for? (A sudden disaster? An eligibility cutoff?)

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Where you are right now
From the pre-workshop survey (9 responses):

7 of 9 are still choosing a topic or have a focus but no question yet, and 6 of 9 haven’t found a dataset. That is normal at this stage.
Biggest obstacles: narrowing the topic and turning a topic into a question data can answer (5 of 9 each).
Most comfortable finding data; least comfortable with correlation and regression (5 of 9: “not at all”).
Top interests: major powers and small states (AOSIS), environmental conflict, NDCs; then climate finance, aid, IOs and North–South divides.
6 of 9 have used R before. Most plan to use Excel, Stata or haven’t decided: today’s ideas carry over to any tool.


Today is built around those obstacles. By the break you should have a draft question. By the end, a first look at data.


~1 min. Survey as of Nov 17 (n = 9). Keep it aggregate; never single out individual responses. Also useful: 3 of 9 lean toward a relationship question and 3 aren’t sure yet; 3 plan to focus on a governance instrument or policy and 4 are undecided on focus. Both come back in the variation slides.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: How do we know what we know?
text:
How do we know what we know?
The course readings use very different kinds of evidence:








Approach
Example from the course
Learns from…




Interviews and observation
Rietig (2014); Ciplet (2019)
How participants experience and explain a process


Process tracing / history
Haas (1992); Benedick (1998)
The sequence of events in one or a few cases


Discourse and document analysis
Lefstad & Paavola (2024)
How actors frame problems


Counting and measuring
Kaya & Schofield (2020); Tennant et al. (2024)
Patterns across many cases





Quantitative work is one way of knowing, not the only one. It is strongest at describing how much, how often, and how things vary across many cases. It is weakest at explaining the mechanisms inside any one case.


~1.5 min. The point: quant and qual are complements. Your 5-page paper is descriptive/correlational quant, and that is a legitimate contribution.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: Numbers are measurements, not the things themselves
text:
Numbers are measurements, not the things themselves


Concept“participation in climate negotiations”


→


Indicatornational delegation size


→


DataUNFCCC lists of participants, COP1–21


→


Number“Country X sent 212 delegates”




Every arrow is a choice someone made, and each choice can be questioned.
Somebody produced the data: a secretariat, a donor, an NGO, a researcher. Why, and with what incentives?
A quantitative claim is an argument: data + assumptions → conclusion. Your job is to make the assumptions visible.


~1.5 min. Example from Kaya & Schofield (Class 2). Ask aloud: does a bigger delegation mean more participation? More influence? Nothing yet about influence.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: What makes a good social-scientific question?
text:
What makes a good social-scientific question?


A good question is…

Answerable with evidence you can actually get
Specific: who, what, where, when
About variation: something differs across cases or over time
Connected to a debate from the course

Descriptive and explanatory questions are both legitimate:

Descriptive: How has X changed? How is X distributed?
Explanatory: Why does X vary? Does Y affect X?


The five question types in your data-paper prompt



Type
Asks…




Change
How has X changed over time?


Distribution
Who gets/has X?


Comparison
How do groups differ?


Composition
What is X made of?


Relationship
Do X and Y move together?



The first four are descriptive. The fifth is about association, which is not yet causation.


~1.5 min. Flag that “relationship” questions are where people slip into causal language. We return to that in a few minutes.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Checkpoint: which question is better?
Raise one hand for A, two hands for B.



1A. Is climate finance fair?


2A. Why do countries pollute?


3A. How did the number of non-state organizations hosting COP side events change after the Paris Agreement?



1B. Did adaptation finance per capita to small island states grow faster than to other developing countries, 2015–2022?


2B. Do countries more dependent on fossil-fuel exports submit less ambitious NDCs?


3B. Are NGOs important in climate governance?




The better question in each pair (1B, 2B, 3A) names a measurable quantity, a set of cases, and a comparison or time frame.


~2 min. Note that 3 flips the order on purpose. For 1A: “fair” is a normative concept. Ask how you’d measure it. That’s the bridge to Measure later.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: Correlation: do two things move together?
text:
Correlation: do two things move together?
A correlation (r) summarizes how closely two variables move together across cases: from −1 (perfectly opposite) through 0 (no straight-line relationship) to +1 (perfectly together). It says nothing about why.

Guess the correlation. Call out your guess for each panel.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Correlation: the answers


~2 min across these two slides. Most people underestimate moderate correlations like B. r = 0.35 is a real but noisy relationship, and many social-science relationships look like B.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Correlation requires variation


To explain a difference, you need a difference. If every country in your data is an AOSIS member, your data cannot tell you what AOSIS membership does.


~1 min. Practical implication for paper design: choose cases that vary on the thing you care about.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Too little variation hides relationships








Cutting the range of X weakens the visible relationship, even though the underlying pattern is the same.

Ask of any dataset: who got left out?

Only countries that received finance?
Only initiatives that survived?
Only events that were registered?




~1.5 min. This sets up Tennant later: eligibility (who gets any finance) vs amount. If you only look at recipients you can miss the selection stage.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: Correlation is not causation: three reasons
text:
Correlation is not causation: three reasons


1. Confounding

A third factor drives both.

2. Reverse causality

The outcome may cause the “cause.”

3. Selection

Cases in the data are not a fair picture of all cases (e.g., only firms that choose to disclose emissions).

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Confounding, in pictures





“Controlling for” state capacity means comparing like with like. It only works for confounders you thought of and measured, and it cannot fix reverse causality.


~1.5 min. Pooled: strong positive. Split by capacity: relationship mostly disappears. This is what regression “controls” do, conceptually.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: Where do credible causal claims come from?
text:
Where do credible causal claims come from?
The core problem: we never see the same country both with and without the “treatment.”
Credible designs find a fair comparison instead:








Design
The idea
Environmental-politics example




Randomized experiment
Chance decides who is treated
Payments to forest owners, randomized across Ugandan villages, reduced deforestation (Jayachandran et al. 2017)


Natural experiment
Nature or history assigns “treatment” as if by chance
Rainfall shocks used to study economic growth and civil conflict (Miguel, Satyanath & Sergenti 2004)


Difference-in-differences
Compare the change in treated vs. untreated units
French manufacturing firms covered by the EU ETS vs. similar uncovered firms, before and after carbon pricing: regulated firms cut CO2 by 14–16% (Colmer et al. 2025)


Regression discontinuity
Compare cases just above vs. just below a cutoff
Design idea: countries just above vs. just below an income threshold for concessional finance





Credibility comes from the design, meaning how the comparison was set up, more than from adding control variables.


~4 min. Don’t teach the methods; teach that they exist and what they buy you. Vanden Eynde & Vargas (Class 12) review this kind of evidence on climate and conflict. Colmer, Martin, Muûls & Wagner (2025), “Does Pricing Carbon Mitigate Climate Change? Firm-Level Evidence from the European Union Emissions Trading System,” Review of Economic Studies 92(3): 1625–1660 (advance access May 2024). Matched difference-in-differences on French administrative data; 14% (phase I) and 16% (phase II) reductions, no detectable drop in output or employment. Verified against the open-access PDF.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: What this means for your data paper
text:
What this means for your data paper

A careful description or correlation is a full, legitimate contribution. Just say what you found, not more.








Instead of…
Write…




“Vulnerability causes countries to receive more finance.”
“More vulnerable countries received more finance on average.”


“Delegation size drives influence.”
“Larger delegations are associated with…”


“This proves…”
“This is consistent with… but could also reflect…”



Name one alternative explanation you can’t rule out. That is what your prompt means by “what you can and cannot conclude.”

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Samples and populations



Population: every case you want to learn about
Sample: the cases you actually observe
Any statistic from a sample (a mean, a correlation) would come out a bit different with a different sample


Let’s watch that happen with a simulated “world” of 150 countries →

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Different samples, different answers


Three random samples of 30 countries give three different means. None of them is “wrong.”

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: The spread of possible answers is the uncertainty
text:
The spread of possible answers is the uncertainty





The standard error measures how much an estimate would bounce around from sample to sample. Bigger samples → smaller standard errors.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Confidence intervals and p-values




95% confidence interval: a procedure that captures the true value in about 95% of samples. (Here, 18 of 20 do.)
p-value: if there were really no relationship, how often would chance alone produce one at least this strong?
A p-value is not…

the probability your hypothesis is true
a measure of how big or important the effect is



~3 min for the whole samples sequence. Statistical significance ≠ substantive significance.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: A puzzle: what if you already have every country?
text:
A puzzle: what if you already have every country?
Many datasets in this course cover (almost) every country: OECD climate finance, UNFCCC participant lists, every COP side event.

Then what does a p-value mean?

Treat the data as one realization of an ongoing process (this year’s allocations could have come out differently)
Or treat the analysis as descriptive: you are reporting what happened, not estimating a hidden truth
Either way, measurement error and who is missing still matter


~1 min. No single right answer. Plant the seed; it comes back with Tennant.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: Recap: six ideas to carry into the papers
text:
Recap: six ideas to carry into the papers

Numbers are measurements of concepts. Every step from concept to number is a choice.
Good questions are specific, answerable, and about variation.
Correlation needs variation, and who is left out of the data shapes what you see.
Correlation ≠ causation: confounding, reverse causality, selection.
Credible causal claims come from design, not from adding controls.
Every estimate comes with uncertainty. Report it honestly and keep statistical and substantive significance apart.

Small groups of 3–4. Everyone has read all three papers. For each paper, every group discusses the same prompts for about 4 minutes, then we hear from a few groups (2–3 minutes).


~1 min. Form groups of 3–4 now and keep them for all three papers. Each part builds on the one before: you can’t map what you haven’t measured, or model what you haven’t mapped. Report-outs: call on a different group each time; ask the others to add only what’s new.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Measure · Fransen et al. (2023)


Measure


Map


Model


The concept: the climate policy implementation gap. The authors split it into two parts:

Policy adoption gap: pledges vs. projected emissions under adopted policies (Climate Action Tracker estimates)
Policy outcome gap: what adopted policies should achieve vs. what they actually achieve. It cannot be measured directly, so they compare policy-strength scores with later outcomes (CCPI)



Who makes these numbers?

Climate Action Tracker: Climate Analytics & NewClimate Institute
CCPI: Germanwatch, NewClimate Institute & CAN, partly from expert assessments


Why it’s a model paper for you

A careful descriptive paper
Openly says the outcome gap is a proxy
Time windows differ across its figures (2014–19, 2018–22, 2023)

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Measure · Discuss in your group

Warm-up, 3 minutes. As a group, pick one concept. Write down: (1) an indicator, (2) a data source, (3) one thing your indicator misses.




Climate ambition of a country
State capacity to implement climate policy
Inclusivity of a COP
Vulnerability to climate change



Then discuss Fransen et al. (4 min), and we’ll hear from a few groups:

How did Fransen et al. get a number for something that “can only be measured after the fact”?
Validity: does a CCPI policy score capture implementation?
Reliability: would different experts score the same country the same way?
Where does the outcome gap show up in the data? (Hint: in the variation around the expected diagonal.)




~12 min total for Measure: ~3 min paper intro, 3 min warm-up, 4 min group discussion, 2–3 min report-out. Collect 2–3 indicators per concept on the board. Then compare: Xie measures inclusivity; Tennant uses vulnerability indices. Key teaching points: validity vs reliability; comparability across countries; numbers made by NGOs/think tanks have their own choices built in.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Map · Xie et al. (2025)


Measure


Map


Model




The data: UNFCCC records of every COP side event, COP9–COP28 (2003–2023): titles, descriptions, host organizations, and who nominated participants
The methods:

Topic modelling (machine learning on event text) to trace themes such as energy, food and forests
Network analysis of who co-hosts energy events with whom (COP17–28)

The pattern: fossil-fuel lobbyists gain access through business NGOs and some governments, and sit at the edge of the anti-fossil-fuel discussion, which grew from a tight network of environmental NGOs.


This is “found data”: administrative records kept for running a conference, repurposed to measure inclusivity.
Mapping is a contribution in itself. No causal claim is needed to make an important point.

In your group, 4 minutes. Then a few groups report back (2–3 minutes).


What is one observation? An event? An organization? A link between organizations?
Population or sample? Every registered side event is included. What isn’t?

Unregistered events, country pavilions, the negotiating rooms themselves…

Model · Tennant, Davies & Tennant (2024)


Measure


Map


Model




Two questions:

Do donors use different criteria to decide who is eligible for climate finance than to decide how much they get?

Two stages:


Findings (from the abstract):

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: Model · Activity: build the causal diagram
text:
Model · Activity: build the causal diagram

Whole class, 5 minutes. What else affects how much climate finance a country receives? I’ll draw it as you call it out.


Starting point. We add arrows together.

Reveal the diagram after students have offered several factors, or draw on the board first and show this as a comparison. Push on: which of these does Tennant control for? Which could still be lurking? Is anything a consequence of finance rather than a cause (reverse causality: does finance build capacity)?

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: Before you climb: where is your variation?
text:
Before you climb: where is your variation?
Every question type needs something that differs. Find yours before you pick a question.







Question type
The variation you need




Change
The same measure in several years


Distribution
Many units that receive or have different amounts


Comparison
At least two groups (or periods), with several cases in each


Composition
A total that splits into parts, and parts that differ in size


Relationship
Variation in both the outcome (Y) and the predictor (X)




~1 min. A relationship question needs both X and Y to vary across the same cases. If your outcome barely varies (every country signed the treaty), there is nothing to explain.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
section: Where variation comes from, by primary focus
text:
Where variation comes from, by primary focus








Your primary focus
Typical unit (one row)
Variation often comes from…




Actor (China, AOSIS, a firm)
Actor-year, or the actor vs. peers
Over time; comparison with similar actors


IO / institution (GCF, World Bank)
Project or recipient
Across projects, recipients, sectors, years


Issue (adaptation, deforestation)
Country or country-year
Across countries and over time


Instrument / policy (NDCs, carbon pricing)
Country or country-year
Adopters vs. non-adopters; before vs. after




One actor = no variation across cases. Get it from time, a comparison group, or the parts of a total.


~1.5 min. The trap: one actor (say, China) gives no cross-sectional variation, so you need time, a comparison group, or a breakdown into parts. Both tables are on the question-ladder worksheet.

title: How Numbers Become Evidence
text:
Climb the ladder









Rung
Example




Topic
Climate finance for small islands


Concept
Access to adaptation finance


Measure
Adaptation-related development finance per capita (OECD), 2015–2022


Pattern
Does it vary across SIDS by income level?


Question

Individually, 5 minutes: write your own five rungs.
In your group, 4 minutes: swap. Your partners check:

Is the measure available?
What varies: over time, across units, or both? (For relationships: do X and Y vary?)
What can’t you conclude?


A few volunteers share (2 min).


~10 min (~12 with the variation slide). Hand out the question-ladder worksheet. Collect ladders (photo or a shared doc) so you can tailor Part 2 examples. The example question is a Comparison question. Point out that it’s descriptive and answerable.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
text:
ImportantBefore you start



Finish the installation guide for your computer first: Mac or Windows.
Goal for tonight: render the test document to HTML and to PDF with Typst. It takes about 20 minutes.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
text:
6.1 Step 1: Download the test document
Download pdf-test.qmd and save it in your pols081 folder. Then open it in RStudio (File → Open File…).
It contains text, a table, a figure made with ggplot2, and some summary statistics, which is everything your data paper will need.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
text:
6.2 Step 2: Look at the header
---
title: "PDF Test for POLS 081"
author: "Your Name"
format:
  typst:
    papersize: us-letter
    margin:
      x: 1in
      y: 1in
    fontsize: 11pt
    toc: false
  html: default
---
Change "Your Name" to your name. The options under typst: control the PDF’s page size, margins and font size.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
text:
6.3 Step 3: Render
Click Render. Because typst is listed first, you’ll get pdf-test.pdf in the same folder. It should open in the Viewer pane or in a separate window.
✅ If you see a PDF with a table and a scatterplot, you’re ready for Wednesday.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
text:
6.4 Step 4 (optional): Try the other formats

Click ▾ next to Render and choose Render HTML.
Change typst to pdf to test the TinyTeX (LaTeX) backup.
Add docx: default to the format list and render a Word document.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
section: 7.1 “dev.control() called without an open graphics device” (Mac)
text:
7.1 “dev.control() called without an open graphics device” (Mac)
This is a Mac graphics problem, not a Typst problem: rendering to HTML fails the same way. Look for warnings underneath that mention X11, libSM.6.dylib or cairo. They mean XQuartz isn’t installed, so R can’t open a graphics device to draw your plot.

Install XQuartz, following the XQuartz step in the Mac guide.
Log out of your Mac and log back in (or restart).
Open RStudio and render again.

Fallback: run install.packages("ragg") in the Console, then add these lines to your document’s YAML header (at the same level as format:) and render again:
knitr:
  opts_chunk:
    dev: ragg_png
See the Mac troubleshooting entry for more detail.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
section: 7.2 “Unknown format: typst” / “typst is not a valid format”
text:
7.2 “Unknown format: typst” / “typst is not a valid format”
Your Quarto is older than 1.4. In the Terminal, run quarto --version.

If it’s below 1.4, you likely have an old, separately installed Quarto (sometimes from Anaconda or VS Code) that RStudio uses instead of its built-in one. Install the latest Quarto from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/, or update RStudio, then restart RStudio.
Don’t confuse this with the R package called quarto, which has its own, different version number. The version that matters is the one printed by quarto --version in the Terminal.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
section: 7.3 “failed to download package” or an error mentioning packages.typst.org
text:
7.3 “failed to download package” or an error mentioning packages.typst.org
Some versions of Quarto download small Typst add-ons (for example, the icons used in callout boxes) the first time you render a PDF.

Make sure you’re connected to the internet (not on a network that blocks downloads) and render again.
Better: update Quarto (or RStudio). Recent versions include these add-ons, so no download is needed.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
section: 7.4 Errors that mention your title, a heading, or a strange character
text:
7.4 Errors that mention your title, a heading, or a strange character
Typst treats some characters as instructions, especially #, $, @, \ and *. In the YAML header (title, author, subtitle), these can break the PDF.

Remove them from your title, or put the whole title in quotes: title: "Climate Finance: 2015–2022".
A $ in text (for example “$100 billion”) is fine in the body, but write it as \$100 billion if you see a math-related error.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
section: 7.5 Errors about an image or figure
text:
7.5 Errors about an image or figure

Typst can’t use web images (URLs) or unusual formats such as .webp or .tiff. Save the image as .png or .jpg in your project folder and reference it by file name.
Check the file name and path: no spaces or accented characters, and the image must be in the folder you point to.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
section: 7.6 “Access is denied”, “permission denied”, or “the file is being used by another process”
text:
7.6 “Access is denied”, “permission denied”, or “the file is being used by another process”
This usually happens on Windows when the PDF is still open in Adobe Acrobat, Edge, or another viewer while Quarto tries to overwrite it.

Close the PDF in every program, then render again.
If your folder is in OneDrive, move it out, or pause syncing.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
text:
7.7 Warnings about fonts (“unknown font family”)
These are warnings, not errors. Typst substitutes a default font and the PDF is still produced. If you added a mainfont: option, remove it or choose a font installed on your computer.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
section: 7.8 Rendering crashes, hangs, or typst “cannot be executed”
text:
7.8 Rendering crashes, hangs, or typst “cannot be executed”

Some antivirus programs (mostly on Windows) block the Typst program that comes with Quarto. Check your antivirus quarantine and allow it.
Close and reopen RStudio, then try again.
Run quarto check in the Terminal. Look for a ✓ next to Typst version. If it’s missing, reinstall the latest Quarto from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
section: 7.9 The R code fails during rendering (but runs when I click ▶)
text:
7.9 The R code fails during rendering (but runs when I click ▶)
When you render, Quarto runs your code in a fresh R session from the folder the .qmd is in. Common causes:

A package is loaded in your Console but not in the document. Add library(tidyverse) (or whichever package) to a chunk near the top.
A data file is referenced with a path that only works from somewhere else. Keep data files in the same folder as the .qmd (or a data/ subfolder) and use relative paths like read_csv("data/mydata.csv").
An object was created in the Console but not in the document. Every object must be created by code in the .qmd.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
section: 7.10 Fallbacks if Typst still won’t work
text:
7.10 Fallbacks if Typst still won’t work

Use LaTeX instead: change typst to pdf in the header (this uses TinyTeX). If TinyTeX isn’t installed, run quarto install tinytex in the Terminal.
Use Word: render to docx, then save as PDF from Word.
Last resort: render to html, open it in your browser, and use Print → Save as PDF.

title: Your First Quarto Document, and Rendering It to PDF
text:
7.11 Still stuck?
Email Greg with:

a screenshot of the error (the first ERROR line in Background Jobs),
your operating system (Mac or Windows, and version), and
the output of quarto check from the Terminal.

If we can’t fix it by email, we’ll work on it during the break on Wednesday.

ImportantDo this before class on Wednesday



Set aside about 30–45 minutes. You’ll install five things, in this order:

RStudio, the program you’ll actually work in (it includes Quarto)
A few R packages

title: Installing R and RStudio on a Mac
text:
4.1 A quick tour
When RStudio opens, you’ll see (usually) four panes:

Console (bottom left): where R runs commands. Type here and press Return.
Source (top left): where you edit scripts and Quarto documents. It appears once you open a file.
Environment / History (top right): the data and objects you’ve created.
Files / Plots / Packages / Help / Viewer (bottom right).

The Console has a sibling tab called Terminal. You’ll use it once below.

title: Installing R and RStudio on a Mac
section: 8.1 “dev.control() called without an open graphics device”
text:
8.1 “dev.control() called without an open graphics device”
You’ll see this when you render a document that makes a plot. The full message looks something like this:
Error in dev.control(displaylist = if (record) "enable" else "inhibit") :
  dev.control() called without an open graphics device
Warning messages:
1: In grSoftVersion() : unable to load shared object
   '.../R.framework/Resources/modules//R_X11.so' ...
   Reason: tried: '/opt/X11/lib/libSM.6.dylib' (no such file) ...
2: In cairoVersion() : unable to load shared object ...
The telltale signs are warnings that mention X11, libSM.6.dylib or /opt/X11, and cairo. They mean XQuartz isn’t installed (or you haven’t logged out and back in since installing it), so R can’t open a graphics device to draw the plot.
Fix:

Install XQuartz (see Install XQuartz).
Log out of your Mac and log back in (or restart).
Open RStudio and render again.







TipFallback if XQuartz still doesn’t help





You can tell R to draw plots with the ragg package, which doesn’t need XQuartz. Run this once in the Console:
install.packages("ragg")
Then add these lines to the YAML header of the document you’re rendering (between the --- lines, at the same level as format:):
knitr:
  opts_chunk:
    dev: ragg_png
Render again. If this works but XQuartz didn’t, email Greg so we can find out why.

title: Installing R and RStudio on a Mac
section: 8.2 “RStudio can’t be opened because Apple cannot check it for malicious software”
text:
8.2 “RStudio can’t be opened because Apple cannot check it for malicious software”

Open System Settings → Privacy & Security.
Scroll down to the Security section. You should see a message about RStudio being blocked.
Click Open Anyway and enter your password.

Alternatively, in Finder, right-click (or Control-click) RStudio in Applications and choose Open.

title: Installing R and RStudio on a Mac
section: 8.3 RStudio says “R not found” or asks you to choose an R installation
text:
8.3 RStudio says “R not found” or asks you to choose an R installation

Make sure you installed R first, then quit RStudio completely (RStudio → Quit, or ⌘Q) and reopen it.
Check that you downloaded the R installer that matches your chip. An arm64 R won’t run on an Intel Mac.
If it still fails, reinstall R, then restart your Mac.

title: Installing R and RStudio on a Mac
section: 8.4 I installed the wrong R (Intel vs. Apple silicon)
text:
8.4 I installed the wrong R (Intel vs. Apple silicon)
Download and install the correct .pkg. It will replace the old version. Then reinstall the packages (see Install the workshop R packages).

title: Installing R and RStudio on a Mac
text:
8.5 My macOS is too old
The simplest fix is to update macOS via System Settings → General → Software Update. Every Apple silicon Mac can run macOS 15 or newer. Updating takes a while, so start early.
If you can’t update before class:

RStudio won’t install or open (macOS 14 or older): install an earlier version of RStudio instead. Posit’s supported versions page includes a table showing which RStudio release works with each version of macOS, and links to those releases. Then run quarto check in RStudio’s Terminal: the Quarto version must be 1.4 or higher for PDFs. If it’s lower, also install the latest Quarto from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/.
R won’t install (Apple silicon on macOS 11–13, or Intel older than macOS 11): older versions of R that support your macOS are available from CRAN. Email Greg and we’ll find the right one.

section: 8.6 “xcrun: error: invalid active developer path” or a message about Command Line Tools
text:
8.6 “xcrun: error: invalid active developer path” or a message about Command Line Tools
This means R tried to compile a package from source. Either:

reinstall the package and answer no when asked about installing from source, or
install Apple’s developer tools by running this in the Terminal and following the prompts (it takes a while):

xcode-select --install

section: 8.7 Package installation fails with “cannot open URL” or “download failed”

In RStudio, go to Tools → Global Options → Packages. Under Primary CRAN repository, click Change…, choose Global (CDN) – Posit, then click OK and try again.

Use the R alternative instead: tinytex::install_tinytex() in the Console. Then restart RStudio.

text:

If quarto check shows a version below 1.4, you probably have an old, separately installed Quarto that RStudio is picking up first. You might have installed it yourself, or it came with Anaconda or VS Code. Either:

text:
ImportantDo this before class on Wednesday



Set aside about 30–45 minutes. You’ll install four things, in this order:

R, the programming language

A few R packages

Then work through the Quarto and PDF guide to check that everything works. If you get stuck, try the troubleshooting section at the bottom of this page first. If that doesn’t solve it, email Greg with a screenshot of the error.

title: Installing R and RStudio on Windows
text:
3.1 A quick tour
When RStudio opens, you’ll see (usually) four panes:

Console (bottom left): where R runs commands. Type here and press Enter.
Source (top left): where you edit scripts and Quarto documents. It appears once you open a file.
Environment / History (top right): the data and objects you’ve created.
Files / Plots / Packages / Help / Viewer (bottom right).

The Console has a sibling tab called Terminal. You’ll use it once below.






WarningDon’t “Run as administrator”



Open RStudio normally, not with right-click → Run as administrator. Running as administrator installs packages into a protected system folder, which causes confusing permission errors later.

title: Installing R and RStudio on Windows
text:
7.1 Installing without administrator rights
This is the most common Windows problem. Here’s the full picture:








Step
With admin rights
Without admin rights




R
Installs to C:\Program Files\R
Click No at the admin prompt. R installs to your own user area (e.g., C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Programs\R)


RStudio
Normal installer
Use the zip version (see the box under Install RStudio)


Packages
Answer Yes to “use a personal library”
Same. Packages go into your personal library automatically


TinyTeX
Installs to your user folder; no admin needed
Same



Symptoms that point to a permissions problem:

Warning in install.packages: 'lib = "C:/Program Files/R/R-4.x.x/library"' is not writable
Error: cannot remove prior installation of package ... or Permission denied
An installer that closes immediately or says “Access is denied”

Fixes:

Re-run install.packages(...) and answer Yes to both “personal library” questions.
Make sure RStudio isn’t being run as administrator (see the warning above).
If a package is “in use” and can’t be updated: close RStudio, reopen it, and install before loading anything (don’t run library() first).

title: Installing R and RStudio on Windows
section: 7.2 RStudio says “R not found” or “R does not appear to be installed”
text:
7.2 RStudio says “R not found” or “R does not appear to be installed”

Make sure you installed R first.
Close RStudio and reopen it. If that doesn’t work, restart your computer so RStudio can find the new installation.
If R was installed somewhere unusual (for example, without admin rights), point RStudio to it: hold Ctrl while opening RStudio. A dialog appears letting you Choose a specific version of R. Select the R folder (look in C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Programs\R\R-4.x.x) and click OK.
Or, if RStudio opens: Tools → Global Options → General → R version → Change…

title: Installing R and RStudio on Windows
section: 7.3 RStudio won’t install or open on Windows 10
text:
7.3 RStudio won’t install or open on Windows 10
The newest version of RStudio supports Windows 11. Microsoft ended regular support for Windows 10 in October 2025, so upgrading (Settings → Windows Update) is the best long-term fix if your computer is eligible.
If you can’t upgrade before class:

Install an earlier version of RStudio from Posit’s supported versions page. Pick the most recent release that installs and opens on your computer.
Open RStudio’s Terminal and run quarto check. The Quarto version must be 1.4 or higher for PDFs.
If it’s lower, also install the latest Quarto from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/, then restart RStudio.

The current R installer still works on Windows 10, so you don’t need to change anything there.

title: Installing R and RStudio on Windows
section: 7.4 Windows Defender / SmartScreen blocks the installer
text:
7.4 Windows Defender / SmartScreen blocks the installer
Click More info → Run anyway. The R and RStudio installers from the official sites are safe. Some antivirus programs also quarantine rstudio.exe or Quarto’s tools. If RStudio flashes and closes immediately, check your antivirus’s quarantine list and allow RStudio.

title: Installing R and RStudio on Windows
section: 7.5 TinyTeX fails, or my username has spaces/accents
text:
7.5 TinyTeX fails, or my username has spaces/accents
TinyTeX (like all LaTeX distributions on Windows) cannot be installed in a path containing non-English characters, and spaces can cause problems too. By default it installs under C:\Users\<yourname>\AppData\Roaming\TinyTeX, so a username like María López breaks it.
Fix: install TinyTeX to a simple folder at the root of C:. In the Console:
install.packages("tinytex")   # make sure tinytex is up to date
tinytex::install_tinytex(dir = "C:/TinyTeX")
Then restart RStudio. You don’t need admin rights to create a folder at C:\.
Other TinyTeX errors such as “The system cannot find the path specified” or “tlmgr returned a non zero status code” usually have the same cause. Try the fix above.






Note



Remember: TinyTeX is only the backup. If it won’t install, you can still make PDFs with Typst. Don’t spend more than 15 minutes on TinyTeX.

section: 7.6 Package installation fails with “cannot open URL” or “download failed”

In RStudio, go to Tools → Global Options → Packages. Under Primary CRAN repository, click Change…, choose Global (CDN) – Posit, then click OK and try again.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
NoteWhat you need



This guide uses only the tidyverse (which includes ggplot2) and the data in the data/ folder of the lab files (Part 2 lab materials). Copy any chunk into a .qmd file in your pols081-lab folder and run it.
Load the tidyverse and the data used on this page:
library(tidyverse)

co2       <- read_csv("data/co2.csv")        # one row per country, 2023
co2_trend <- read_csv("data/co2_trend.csv")  # one row per country per year, 2018-2023
aid       <- read_csv("data/adaptation_aid.csv") %>%
  mutate(aid_pc = adapt_aid_musd * 1000000 / population)
About colors. We use R’s color names, such as "steelblue", "darkorange" and "seagreen". R knows hundreds of them (full list of R color names), and you can use any of them directly in ggplot().

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
1.1 Change: a line chart
A line connects the years in order, so the eye follows the trend. Use it when the x-axis is time.

co2_trend %>%
  filter(country %in% c("China", "Germany", "United States")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = co2_pc, color = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("China" = "darkorange", "Germany" = "seagreen",
                                "United States" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(title = "CO2 emissions per person",
       x = NULL, y = "Tonnes of CO2 per person", color = NULL,
       caption = "Source: World Bank WDI (EDGAR).") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: CO2 per person in three large emitters, 2018–2023.





filter(country %in% c(...)) keeps just the countries we want. With more than four or five lines, a chart gets hard to read: pick the cases your question is about.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
1.2 Distribution: a histogram (or boxplot)
A histogram sorts countries into bins and counts them, so you can see where most cases sit and how far the tail stretches.

ggplot(co2, aes(x = co2_pc)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "CO2 emissions per person, 2023",
       x = "Tonnes of CO2 per person", y = "Number of countries",
       caption = "Source: World Bank WDI (EDGAR).") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 2: Most countries emit a few tonnes of CO2 per person; a few emit far more.





Try a few values of binwidth: too wide hides the shape, too narrow makes it noisy. A boxplot (next section) shows the same spread more compactly.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
section: 1.3 Comparison: bars of group summaries, or boxplots
text:
1.3 Comparison: bars of group summaries, or boxplots
To compare groups, first summarize each group (here, the median), then draw one bar per group. Bar length is easy to compare, so bars must start at zero.

co2 %>%
  group_by(income_group) %>%
  summarize(median_co2_pc = median(co2_pc)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(income_group, median_co2_pc), y = median_co2_pc)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "The typical country's CO2 per person, by income group",
       x = NULL, y = "Median tonnes of CO2 per person",
       caption = "Source: World Bank WDI (EDGAR), 2023.") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 3: Median CO2 per person by World Bank income group.





A bar shows only one number per group. A boxplot shows the whole spread in each group: the thick line is the median and the box holds the middle half of the countries.

ggplot(co2, aes(x = reorder(income_group, co2_pc), y = co2_pc)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(title = "CO2 per person, by income group",
       x = NULL, y = "Tonnes of CO2 per person",
       caption = "Source: World Bank WDI (EDGAR), 2023.") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4: The same comparison as a boxplot, showing the spread within each group.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
1.4 Composition: a proportional bar
A composition question asks what share of a total each part makes up. Here we compare two totals, the world’s population and its CO2 emissions, split by income group. position = "fill" stretches each bar to 100%, so the segments are shares.

co2 %>%
  group_by(income_group) %>%
  summarize(Population = sum(population),
            `CO2 emissions` = sum(co2_mt)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Population, `CO2 emissions`),
               names_to = "total", values_to = "amount") %>%
  mutate(income_group = factor(income_group,
                               levels = c("High income", "Upper middle income",
                                          "Lower middle income", "Low income"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = total, y = amount, fill = income_group)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Low income" = "seagreen",
                               "Lower middle income" = "steelblue",
                               "Upper middle income" = "darkorange",
                               "High income" = "grey30")) +
  labs(title = "Shares of world population and CO2 emissions, 2023",
       x = NULL, y = "Share of the total", fill = NULL,
       caption = "Source: World Bank WDI (EDGAR).") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 5: High-income countries hold a small share of the world’s people but a large share of its emissions.





pivot_longer() turns the two total columns into rows, one per income group and total, which is the shape ggplot() needs to stack them. factor() with levels puts the income groups in a meaningful order; otherwise R sorts them alphabetically.






TipWhy not a pie chart?



People judge lengths along a common scale much more accurately than angles or areas. In a pie, slices of similar size are hard to tell apart, and comparing two pies side by side is harder still. A stacked or proportional bar shows the same shares and makes comparisons easy.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
1.5 Relationship: a scatterplot
A scatterplot puts one dot per case, with one variable on each axis. It shows whether the two variables move together, and how tightly.

ggplot(aid, aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkorange") +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000),
                labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000")) +
  labs(title = "Vulnerability and adaptation aid per person",
       x = "ND-GAIN vulnerability (higher = more vulnerable)",
       y = "Aid per person, US$ (log scale)",
       caption = "Source: OECD Rio markers; ND-GAIN; World Bank.") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 6: More vulnerable countries receive somewhat more adaptation aid per person.





geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a straight trend line. Remember from Part 1: a relationship is not causation. Confounding, reverse causality and selection can all produce a pattern like this (Part 1 slides: correlation is not causation).

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
2.1 Step 1: an empty canvas

ggplot(aid)







Figure 7: Step 1: ggplot(aid) sets up an empty canvas.





ggplot() says which data to use, but nothing more, so R draws a blank panel. Every plot starts here.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
section: 2.2 Step 2: map variables to the axes
text:
2.2 Step 2: map variables to the axes

ggplot(aid) +
  aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc)







Figure 8: Step 2: aes() maps variables to the x and y axes.





aes() (short for aesthetics) maps columns to parts of the plot. Now R knows the axes and their ranges, but there are still no marks.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
2.3 Step 3: add marks

ggplot(aid) +
  aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc) +
  geom_point()







Figure 9: Step 3: geom_point() draws one dot per country.





A geom_ (geometric object) draws the data. Most dots are squashed at the bottom because a few countries get far more aid per person than the rest. A log scale spreads them out; each gridline is ten times the one below:

ggplot(aid) +
  aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000),
                labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000"))







Figure 10: Step 3b: scale_y_log10() spreads out the skewed values.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
section: 2.4 Step 4: labels and a source line
text:
2.4 Step 4: labels and a source line

ggplot(aid) +
  aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000),
                labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000")) +
  labs(title = "Vulnerability and adaptation aid per person",
       x = "ND-GAIN vulnerability (higher = more vulnerable)",
       y = "Aid per person, US$ (log scale)",
       caption = "Source: OECD Rio markers; ND-GAIN; World Bank; UN M49.")







Figure 11: Step 4: labs() adds a title, plain-language axis labels and a source.





Replace column names like aid_pc with words a reader understands, include units, and say when an axis is logged. The caption is your source line.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
2.5 Step 5: color by group

ggplot(aid) +
  aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc, color = sids) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000),
                labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Other = "steelblue", SIDS = "darkorange")) +
  labs(title = "Vulnerability and adaptation aid per person",
       x = "ND-GAIN vulnerability (higher = more vulnerable)",
       y = "Aid per person, US$ (log scale)", color = NULL,
       caption = "Source: OECD Rio markers; ND-GAIN; World Bank; UN M49.")







Figure 12: Step 5: aes(color = sids) colors the dots by group; scale_color_manual() picks the colors.





Putting color = sids inside aes() maps a column to color, so R adds a legend. scale_color_manual() sets which color goes with which group. (To make every dot the same color instead, put color = "steelblue" inside geom_point(), outside aes().)

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
2.6 Step 6: a trend line

ggplot(aid) +
  aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc, color = sids) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000),
                labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Other = "steelblue", SIDS = "darkorange")) +
  labs(title = "Vulnerability and adaptation aid per person",
       x = "ND-GAIN vulnerability (higher = more vulnerable)",
       y = "Aid per person, US$ (log scale)", color = NULL,
       caption = "Source: OECD Rio markers; ND-GAIN; World Bank; UN M49.")







Figure 13: Step 6: geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a straight trend line for each group, with a shaded band.





method = "lm" fits a straight line. Because color is mapped to sids, we get one line per group. The shaded band (se = TRUE) is a 95% confidence interval for the line: the range of lines that fit the data about as well. A wide band, like the one for SIDS, means we’re unsure where the line really is, here because there are few SIDS and they are spread out.

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
2.7 Step 7: a theme

ggplot(aid) +
  aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc, color = sids) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000),
                labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Other = "steelblue", SIDS = "darkorange")) +
  labs(title = "Vulnerability and adaptation aid per person",
       x = "ND-GAIN vulnerability (higher = more vulnerable)",
       y = "Aid per person, US$ (log scale)", color = NULL,
       caption = "Source: OECD Rio markers; ND-GAIN; World Bank; UN M49.") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 14: Step 7: theme_minimal() removes the grey background.





A theme controls the look: background, gridlines, fonts. theme_minimal() is clean and works well in a paper. Others to try: theme_bw(), theme_classic().

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
2.8 Step 8 (optional): small multiples

ggplot(aid) +
  aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc, color = sids) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000),
                labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Other = "steelblue", SIDS = "darkorange")) +
  facet_wrap(~ sids) +
  labs(title = "Vulnerability and adaptation aid per person",
       x = "ND-GAIN vulnerability (higher = more vulnerable)",
       y = "Aid per person, US$ (log scale)",
       caption = "Source: OECD Rio markers; ND-GAIN; World Bank; UN M49.") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Figure 15: Step 8: facet_wrap(~ sids) draws one panel per group.





facet_wrap(~ sids) splits the plot into small multiples, one panel per group, with the same axes. That makes each group easier to see when dots overlap. Since the panel titles now name the groups, we hide the legend with theme(legend.position = "none").

title: Choosing and Building a Visualization
text:
2.9 Step 9: save the figure
Inside a Quarto document you don’t need to save anything: the figure appears in your PDF when you render. To use a figure somewhere else (a Word or Google Doc, or slides), store the plot in an object and save it with ggsave():

my_plot <- ggplot(aid) +
  aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc, color = sids) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Vulnerability and adaptation aid per person") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("aid-vulnerability.png", plot = my_plot,
       width = 6.5, height = 4, dpi = 300)

This writes aid-vulnerability.png into your project folder. width and height are in inches; dpi = 300 makes it sharp enough to print.






TipCross-references



Each figure on this page has a label starting with fig- and a caption, set in the first lines of the chunk:
```{r}
#| label: fig-aid
#| fig-cap: "Vulnerability and adaptation aid per person."
ggplot(...)
```
Then write @fig-aid in your text, and Quarto turns it into a numbered link, like this one to Figure 13. Numbers update automatically if you add or move figures.

Build the measure you need
Large countries get more aid in total simply because they have more people. Make a per-person measure:

text:
Correlation test

cor.test(aid$vulnerability, log(aid$aid_pc))


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  aid$vulnerability and log(aid$aid_pc)
t = 3.2341, df = 132, p-value = 0.001542
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1062558 0.4211952
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.2709616 



~4 min. Read three things: the correlation (cor), the 95% CI, the p-value. We use log(aid_pc) because a few extreme values drive an ordinary correlation, and to match the log-scale figure. Recall from Part 1: the p-value asks “if there were no relationship, how often would chance alone produce one this strong?”

title: From Data to Evidence
text:
Comparing two means: t-test

t.test(aid_pc ~ sids, data = aid)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  aid_pc by sids
t = -2.2527, df = 30.03, p-value = 0.03174
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Other and group SIDS is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -241.80448  -11.85043
sample estimates:
mean in group Other  mean in group SIDS 
           9.832621          136.660076 



~3 min. The formula reads “aid per person, by SIDS status.” Look at the two group means, the CI for the difference, the p-value. A big difference with a wide CI: the SIDS group is small and very spread out.

title: From Data to Evidence
section: What the test can’t tell you
text:
What the test can’t tell you



Confounding: SIDS are small, and small countries get more per person. Vulnerability, size, or donor ties?
Selection: only countries that received adaptation aid are in the data. Tennant’s eligibility stage is invisible.



Measurement: donors tag their own projects; “significant” projects count in full.
Inference: we have nearly every recipient. The p-value is about chance in allocations, not about a bigger population.



A small p-value says chance alone is an unlikely explanation. It doesn’t say why, and it doesn’t say how much it matters.


~3 min. Straight callback to the Part 1 recap: confounding, selection, measurement, uncertainty.

Issue
Sources

OECD Data Explorer: search “Rio markers” or “climate-related development finance” (aid by donor, recipient, year and adaptation/mitigation) · Climate Funds Update · UNFCCC biennial reports

Ember electricity data · Our World in Data: energy · World Bank WDI (renewables share; note that it counts firewood and charcoal)


Critical minerals
USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (production and reserves by country)


Fossil-fuel dependence and subsidies
World Bank WDI (fuel exports as % of merchandise exports; oil, gas and coal rents) · IMF fossil fuel subsidies


Environmental conflict
Uppsala Conflict Data Program downloads





A governance instrument or policy
NDCs, carbon pricing, emissions trading, climate-related development finance, voluntary carbon markets, environmental provisions in trade agreements.



Instrument
Sources




NDCs
UNFCCC NDC registry (the documents) · Climate Watch (NDC content coded and comparable) · Climate Action Tracker (ratings)

World Bank Carbon Pricing Dashboard · ICAP ETS map


Climate laws and policies
Climate Change Laws of the World · Climate Policy Database · CCPI (policy scores; used by Fransen et al. 2023)


Climate-related development finance
OECD Data Explorer (Rio markers)


Voluntary carbon markets
Berkeley Carbon Trading Project: Voluntary Registry Offsets Database


Environmental provisions in trade agreements
TREND: Trade and Environment Database



Tip. Policy questions often compare adopters and non-adopters, or before and after adoption. Remember from Part 1: that comparison is descriptive unless you have a design that rules out other explanations.
